newsitem.title: USA: Pork prices soar after pig report.
newsitem.headline: Pork prices soar after pig report.

text.p: A drop in the government's estimate of the U.S. hog population sent pork futures prices soaring Monday, while driving grain prices lower.
Late Friday, the Department of Agriculture estimated that as of Dec. 1, U.S. farms held 56.34 million hogs and pigs, down 4 percent from a year earlier.
Moreover, the number of hogs being kept for breeding purposes fell to 6.76 million animals, down 3 percent from last year and 6 percent from two years ago.
Ron Plain, a University of Missouri agricultural economist, said producers in the Midwest did not have enough faith in the future of hog prices to enlarge herds.
"They possibly think there is a better future in selling corn then feeding it to hogs," he said.
Some traders said they expected the large shrinkage in the hog herd to be revised in future reports. But the reaction of agricultural markets to the smaller pork supply was immediate.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, hog contracts closed up the daily 2.00 cent per pound trading limit as far out as the April 1998 delivery period. February hogs closed at 79.50 cents, a new life-of-contract high.
Prices of pork bellies, used to make bacon, also soared, with all contracts rising the allowable 3.00 cent-a-pound daily limit. February pork bellies ended at 80.425 cents a pound.
Buoyed by the gains in pork, prices of live and feeder cattle also rose. February live cattle ended at 65.875 cents a pound, up 1.075 cents, and January feeder cattle at 68.200 cents, up 1.325 cents.

Partly fuelling those gains were sharp losses in Chicago Board of Trade grain prices, sparked by the indicated drop in the population of hogs. Hog farmers are major users of corn, soy meal and other feed grains.
March corn fell 6-1/4 cents a bushel to $2.58-1/4.
Wheat prices also plunged after the lowest weekly export inspections estimate since 1982 was issued by the Agriculture Department. March wheat closed at $3.82, down 7-1/2 cents.

The government said for the week ended Dec. 26 wheat inspected for export totalled 4.5 million bushels, the lowest since 1982, when the Agriculture Department began keeping computerized records, and far below last week's 13.5 million bushels.
Even including the Christmas holiday, traders said the figure confirmed fears that U.S. wheat was overvalued.
U.S. soft red winter wheat Monday was selling for $159.35 per ton at the Gulf of Mexico, compared with Argentina's prices of around $145, export traders said.
January soybeans closed 7-1/4 cents a bushel lower at $6.94-1/4 due to good growing weather in South American fields. January soy meal closed $2.40 a ton lower at $228.50, following soybeans.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude and heating oil prices edged higher, tracking a rally sparked by arctic weather in Europe that increased demand for heating oil.
"We were up mainly because of London, though fundamentally there was no other news to push us up today," said Bill O'Grady, energy analyst with A.G. Edwards.
February crude oil closed 15 cents a barrel higher at $25.37. January heating oil ended 0.02 cent a gallon higher at 70.57 cents, but January gasoline ended 0.13 cent lower at 69.61 cents a gallon.
A deep freeze gripped Europe, sending temperatures below zero in many regions and blanketing the Mediterranean isle of Corsica with the heaviest snowfall in a decade.
But temperatures in much of the Midwest and Northeast rose, moderating heating demand.
